title: Hamster
wiki_lead:
Hamsters are rodents (order Rodentia) belonging to the subfamily Cricetinae, which contains 19 species classified in seven genera. They have become established as popular small pets. The best-known species of hamster is the golden or Syrian hamster (Mesocricetus auratus), which is the type most commonly kept as a pet. Other hamster species commonly kept as pets are the three species of dwarf hamster, Campbell's dwarf hamster (Phodopus campbelli), the winter white dwarf hamster (Phodopus sungorus, also commonly known as Djungarian hamster) and the Roborovski hamster (Phodopus roborovskii), and the less common Chinese hamster (Cricetulus griseus).
Hamsters feed primarily on seeds, fruits, vegetation, and occasionally burrowing insects. In the wild, they are crepuscular: they forage during the twilight hours. In captivity, however, they are known to live a conventionally nocturnal lifestyle, waking around sundown to feed and exercise. Physically, they are stout-bodied with distinguishing features that include elongated cheek pouches extending to their shoulders, which they use to carry food back to their burrows, as well as a short tail and fur-covered feet.

The best-known species of hamster is the golden or Syrian hamster (Mesocricetus auratus), which is the type most commonly kept as a pet. In captivity, however, they are known to live a conventionally nocturnal lifestyle, waking around sundown to feed and exercise. Physically, they are stout-bodied with distinguishing features that include elongated cheek pouches extending to their shoulders, which they use to carry food back to their burrows, as well as a short tail and fur-covered feet.


Classification

The hamster subfamily Cricetinae forms part of the broader family Cricetidae, that also includes voles, lemmings and muskrats (all of which are in Arvicolinae), and New World rats and mice (Neotominae, Sigmodontinae and Tylomyinae). Within Cricetidae, Hamsters are most closely related to Arvicolinae. Cricetidae is placed as part of the broader clade Muroidea, within which Cricetidae is most closely related to Muridae, which includes Murinae (the Old World rats and mice), and gerbils (Gerbillinae) among others.
The earliest hamsters appeared during the Middle Miocene, around 15 million years ago, with the origin of the group likely being in central or eastern Europe, reaching eastern Asia by around 10 million years ago. A 2026 phylogenetic analysis found that the ancestor of all living hamsters probably only lived around 5-6 million years ago at the end of the Miocene, probably somewhere around southeast Europe or West Asia.

grok_lead: Hamsters are small rodents belonging to the subfamily Cricetinae within the family Cricetidae and order Rodentia, comprising approximately 18 to 26 species classified in seven to nine genera. They are native to the Palearctic region, including central and eastern Europe, the Middle East, and Asia north of the Himalayas, inhabiting diverse environments such as steppes, deserts, forests, and agricultural fields. Distinguished by their short tails, stubby legs, small ears, and expandable cheek pouches for hoarding food, hamsters are primarily nocturnal burrowers that construct complex underground tunnels for shelter, nesting, and storing caches of seeds and vegetation. Their omnivorous diet includes grains, fruits, insects, and occasionally small vertebrates, supporting their high-energy foraging lifestyle. While most species remain wild and solitary outside breeding periods, certain ones like the Syrian or golden hamster ( Mesocricetus auratus)âfirst domesticated from a litter discovered in Syria in 1930âhave become widely kept as pets due to their manageable size, adaptability to captivity, and utility in biomedical research for modeling diseases and genetics. Typical lifespans range from 1.5 to 3 years in captivity, though wild populations face threats from habitat loss and predation.
